### Matching the cell to `torch.nn.RNN` `torch.nn.RNN` implements the recurrent feature extractor. It does not include the embedding table or the vocabulary classifier of `RNNLM`. For one unidirectional layer with `batch_first=True`, the shapes are | Object | Shape | Meaning | |---|---|---| | Input | `[B,T,d]` | Feature vectors, not token IDs | | `output` | `[B,T,m]` | Hidden state at every position | | `h_0`, `h_n` | `[1,B,m]` | Initial and final state of the layer | `batch_first` changes the input/output layout, not the hidden-state layout. With several layers, the leading state axis enumerates layers; `output` contains the top layer’s sequence. These contracts and the equivalent recurrence are specified in [PyTorch 2.14, RNN](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/2.14/generated/torch.nn.RNN.html). ### Two biases represent one effective offset The library cell has input and recurrent biases, `bias_ih_l0` and `bias_hh_l0`. Both are added before the same tanh. To match our cell, copy its $b_h$ to the first and set the second to zero. The forward pass then depends on their sum, $b_{\mathrm{eff}}=b_{ih}+b_{hh}$. The following complete example uses the same $d=3$, $m=4$ dimensions. It compares every state and the input/initial-state gradients, then checks the two bias derivatives. The input vectors are assigned random features here; no embedding lookup or language-model loss is implied. ```python import torch torch.manual_seed(31) dtype = torch.float64 B, T, d, m = 2, 4, 3, 4 features = torch.randn(B, T, d, dtype=dtype, requires_grad=True) initial_state = torch.randn(1, B, m, dtype=dtype, requires_grad=True) input_weight = (.1 * torch.randn(m, d, dtype=dtype)).requires_grad_() state_weight = (.1 * torch.randn(m, m, dtype=dtype)).requires_grad_() single_bias = torch.randn(m, dtype=dtype, requires_grad=True) cell = torch.nn.RNN(d, m, batch_first=True, dtype=dtype) with torch.no_grad(): cell.weight_ih_l0.copy_(input_weight) cell.weight_hh_l0.copy_(state_weight) cell.bias_ih_l0.copy_(single_bias) cell.bias_hh_l0.zero_() state = initial_state[0] history = [] for t in range(T): state = torch.tanh(features[:, t] @ input_weight.T + state @ state_weight.T + single_bias) history.append(state) manual_states = torch.stack(history, dim=1) library_states, library_final = cell(features, initial_state) torch.testing.assert_close(library_states, manual_states) torch.testing.assert_close(library_final, manual_states[:, -1][None]) assert library_states.shape == (B, T, m) assert library_final.shape == (1, B, m) manual_gradients = torch.autograd.grad(manual_states.square().sum(), (features, initial_state, input_weight, state_weight, single_bias)) library_gradients = torch.autograd.grad(library_states.square().sum(), (features, initial_state, cell.weight_ih_l0, cell.weight_hh_l0, cell.bias_ih_l0, cell.bias_hh_l0)) for got, expected in zip(library_gradients[:4], manual_gradients[:4]): torch.testing.assert_close(got, expected) for got in library_gradients[4:]: torch.testing.assert_close(got, manual_gradients[4]) g = manual_gradients[4] rate = .01 effective_after_two_biases = (cell.bias_ih_l0.detach() + cell.bias_hh_l0.detach() - rate * (library_gradients[4] + library_gradients[5])) torch.testing.assert_close(effective_after_two_biases, single_bias.detach() - 2 * rate * g) assert not torch.allclose(effective_after_two_biases, single_bias.detach() - rate * g) ``` If $g=\partial L/\partial b_{\mathrm{eff}}$, then each bias receives the same $g$. For plain SGD with rate $\eta$, updating both changes their sum by $-2\eta g$. Updating one bias changes it by $-\eta g$. Equal forward values therefore do not imply identical optimizer steps. This calculation has no clipping, momentum or weight decay. Our recurrent core has $md+m^2+m=32$ parameters. The library core has $md+m^2+2m=36$. Keeping the same embedding and output classifier would give 100 parameters instead of 96. To preserve the single-bias parameterization when using this module, the extra bias can be held at zero rather than trained. Time sharing of a weight and splitting a bias into two trainable parameters are separate choices. ## BPTT: backpropagation по развёрнутой сети

### Variable-length batches without PAD state updates Consider three independent sequences of lengths 2, 4 and 1. Call their input vectors $A_0,A_1$, $B_0,\ldots,B_3$ and $C_0$. For packing, descending length order is B, A, C. The active rows are | Time | Active rows | Packed input vectors | |---:|---|---| | 0 | B, A, C | $B_0,A_0,C_0$ | | 1 | B, A | $B_1,A_1$ | | 2 | B | $B_2$ | | 3 | B | $B_3$ | The packed data contain seven vectors instead of twelve padded slots. `batch_sizes` is `[3,2,1,1]`: the number of active sequences at each step. This is a time-grouped layout, not three complete sequences concatenated one after another. A row that has ended does not receive another RNN update. [`pack_padded_sequence`](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/2.14/generated/torch.nn.utils.rnn.pack_padded_sequence.html) accepts unsorted input with `enforce_sorted=False`. Tensor lengths must be on the CPU. They select valid prefixes: this interface is not a mask for left padding or holes inside a sequence. In the example below, all lengths are positive and no greater than the padded width. ```python import torch from torch.nn.utils.rnn import pack_padded_sequence, pad_packed_sequence torch.manual_seed(11) dtype = torch.float64 lengths = torch.tensor([2, 4, 1], dtype=torch.int64) # CPU, original row order valid = torch.arange(4)[None, :] < lengths[:, None] inputs = torch.randn(3, 4, 3, dtype=dtype) inputs[~valid] = 0. # Even zero PAD features do not freeze a dense RNN. network = torch.nn.RNN(3, 4, batch_first=True, dtype=dtype) packed = pack_padded_sequence(inputs, lengths, batch_first=True, enforce_sorted=False) assert packed.batch_sizes.tolist() == [3, 2, 1, 1] assert packed.data.shape == (7, 3) packed_output, packed_final = network(packed) output, restored_lengths = pad_packed_sequence( packed_output, batch_first=True, total_length=4) torch.testing.assert_close(restored_lengths, lengths) assert output.shape == (3, 4, 4) and packed_final.shape == (1, 3, 4) assert output[~valid].count_nonzero() == 0 dense_output, dense_final = network(inputs) for row, length in enumerate(lengths.tolist()): short_output, short_final = network(inputs[row:row+1, :length]) torch.testing.assert_close(output[row, :length], short_output[0]) torch.testing.assert_close(packed_final[:, row:row+1], short_final) torch.testing.assert_close(dense_output[row, length-1], short_final[0, 0]) if length < inputs.shape[1]: assert not torch.allclose(dense_final[:, row], packed_final[:, row]) ``` The packed final state matches running each short sequence separately, in the original A, B, C row order. In the dense run, selecting `dense_output[row, length-1]` also recovers that state for this unidirectional network. Taking `dense_final` instead includes the extra PAD-time transitions for the short rows. [`pad_packed_sequence`](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/2.14/generated/torch.nn.utils.rnn.pad_packed_sequence.html) restores the original row order; `total_length=4` fixes the unpacked width. The zeros it inserts into `output` are padding values, not computed states after fictitious tokens. When computing a loss on this unpacked tensor, the valid-position mask is still required. Packing does not reset states between documents and does not detach the computational graph at a chunk boundary. ### Ограничения рекуррентной модели Остаются три разных ограничения.
